1: Alcohol: your fitness to drive is impaired considerably from 0.3 per mille (30 mg per 100 ml of blood). Even small amounts can delay reactions, cause reckless driving and impair hearing and vision.
A drunk driver cannot get fit again quickly. Half an hour of sleep, two cups of strong coffee or a half-hour walk do not help. A blood alcohol of 1.0 per mille takes about 10 hours to clear.
Alcohol hits harder with sleeping pills, pain killers or sedatives, on an empty stomach, or when drinks are downed quickly.

Drugs (hashish, marijuana/dagga, heroin, cocaine, LSD, amphetamines) can make you unfit to drive even after one use. Hashish traces show in urine weeks later, and its effects include misjudging speed and distance and poor attention.
People who take drugs regularly are unfit to drive even when not high. A drug-dependent person is fit again only after proving a whole year without drugs and no likelihood of relapse.
Driving on drugs can cost you your licence (confiscation or ban), a fine and/or imprisonment, and a compulsory medical or psychological examination.
Tiredness: heavy eyelids, feeling chilly and sudden frights mean stop and take a proper break. Plan rests on long journeys and do some exercises at stops.

Distractions: telephone, lighting a cigarette, nagging children, strong emotions, lively conversation, gripping radio programmes. Loud radio, headphones and a loud exhaust ("power sound") stop you hearing sirens and warnings.
Never drive when furious. Time pressure never excuses ignoring traffic rules. If a young driver revs beside you at the lights, ignore the challenge and stay cool.
A good driver treats others like partners, drives calmly and coolly and never shows off. If someone cuts into your lane or tailgates, stay calm and let faster drivers overtake.
2: Road traffic needs caution at all times and consideration for others. You must reckon with improper conduct by others and drive with foresight.
Defensive driving means not insisting on your rights and allowing for other people's mistakes.
Unnecessary obstruction: stalling in dense traffic, driving too slowly for no good reason, running out of fuel.

Things that cause dangerous situations: cutting corners, dipping headlights too late, brakes that grab on one side, too much steering-wheel play, worn tyres, headlights set too high, a broken-down vehicle not marked as required, excessive speed.
3: Carry your driving licence and the vehicle registration certificate.

Bought a registered vehicle: have it re-registered immediately and submit proof of insurance. Sold one: tell the registration centre the buyer's name and address and hand over the registration papers against a receipt. (Stencil Test 4 Q3 words this differently, see the note in that question.)
Number plates: fixed securely in the right places, always easily legible, rear plate lit in darkness, and nothing on them may be changed.

The test stamp and the entry in the registration certificate show when the next inspection is due. A new car is first inspected after 3 years. A second-hand car just inspected is due again after 2 years.

Exhaust test: petrol with catalytic converter every 2 years, petrol without a converter every 12 months, diesel every 2 years. The hexagonal stamp on the front plate shows the date of the next exhaust test.
A caravan trailer left standing for six months still has to meet the deadline on its test stamp.

After a technical change needing an expert opinion, carry the opinion certificate with the new roadworthiness report and have the vehicle document corrected. A lowered suspension needs the expert opinion immediately after the alteration.
Alterations that cancel the permit for use bring a fine, demerit points in the traffic offender file, and the insurance cover lapses.
No motor liability insurance: the vehicle may not be used on the road and must be de-registered at the registration centre.
4: Slow farm tractors, working machines, mopeds and invalid carriages should use the hard shoulder where possible. The left-hand hard shoulder may be used for stopping and parking and for slow vehicles.
Never drive along the broken white centre line in fog. It endangers oncoming traffic.
On a road with three lanes each way, with traffic well spaced in the far left lane, you may stay in the middle lane. Inside built-up areas, vehicles up to 3.5 t may choose their lane freely.
You may only drive faster in the left-hand lane than in the right when queues have formed or when the lane arrows point in different directions.
Highway overtaking accidents come from not watching the traffic behind and from driving too close to the vehicle in front. You may not overtake on the left when there is no queue in the right lane.

Leaving a Highway: indicate in good time, use the left-hand lane early enough, and slow down on the exit lane (after a long drive at 120 km/h check your speedometer, because you underestimate your speed).
Joining: Highway traffic has priority. Accelerate in the acceleration lane, filter in, and if you cannot join stop toward the end of the lane. Never force your way.
Tailgated by a driver flashing lights: move over to the left lane as soon as possible. If you miss your exit, drive on to the next one.
On a Highway: no U-turns, no reversing, no stopping on the roadway or hard shoulder. Highway vehicles need a documented top speed of more than 60 km/h.

Traffic jam: make a channel for emergency vehicles. On three lanes the channel goes between the right-hand and middle lane. On two lanes, right-lane vehicles keep right and left-lane vehicles keep left.
Broken down on a Highway: leave at the next exit when towed, with hazard lights on both vehicles.
5: Built-up areas: 60 km/h. Roads outside built-up areas with one marked lane each way: cars 120 km/h. Car with trailer: 80 km/h. Trucks and combinations (7.5 t, 8 t with trailer, 3.6 t with trailer): 80 km/h. Twin-wheel vehicles: 80 km/h. On a clearway sign "recommended 100", a car with trailer still max 80.

Fog with 50 m visibility: maximum 50 km/h. If you can see 50 m on a narrow road, you must be able to stop within 25 m. You must always be able to stop within the range of vision, or of your dipped headlights at night.

Reaction distance = speed/10 x 3 (1 s reaction): 30 m at 100 km/h, 18 m at 60 km/h, 15 m at 50 km/h. Braking distance = (speed/10) x (speed/10): 100 m at 100, 36 m at 60, 25 m at 50. Stopping distance = reaction + braking: 130 m at 100, 54 m at 60, 40 m at 50.
Double the speed and the braking distance is 4 times as long. A pedestrian steps out 20 m ahead: at 40 km/h a collision cannot be avoided.
Braking distance gets longer with a trailer without brakes, wet or slippery roads, downhill slopes, bad tyres and weak brakes.

Safe distance outside built-up areas: half the speedometer reading in metres. In a 50 km/h urban stream: 15 m, about 3 car lengths. Increase it in rain, fog and on wet roads (wheel-spray, longer braking, greasy film).
Rear-end collisions come from unexpected heavy braking, inattentiveness, and driving too close. Cars with foreign plates may brake or stop suddenly to ask the way.

Skids and bends: reduce speed before the bend, accelerate only when the road straightens. Heavy braking and wet roads cause skids. Front-wheel drive pushes the front end out if you accelerate too hard, rear-wheel drive pushes the rear out. Centrifugal force at 60 km/h is 4 times that at 30.
Aquaplaning (sliding on a water film): high speed, worn tyres, grooves and dips make it likely, and you can no longer steer or brake.
Strong side wind: steer against it and slow down. Expect it on bridges, behind cuttings and when passing trucks (slipstream). Gaps in forests and fire breaks are danger spots too.
Muddy stretch: avoid accelerating, braking and sudden steering movements. Dirt on the road is likely near construction sites and farm-track junctions. After rain on a dry road, expect a greasy film.
Sudden fog appears near rivers, lakes and marshy areas. Adapt your speed and switch on dipped headlights.
Driving fast for a long time makes you lose your feel for speed. You also underestimate speed on wide, good roads with no trees or buildings at the edge.

Fast driving is most dangerous at blind spots, road narrowings, level crossings, crossroads, pedestrian crossings and bends. In residential areas expect children, doors opening and vehicles pulling out.
Horn: a warning signal only (and an overtaking signal outside built-up areas). Hazard lights warn of broken-down vehicles, school buses with children boarding or alighting, and traffic jams.
6: No signs at a crossroads or junction: "right before left", the vehicle from the right goes first. Unclear? Wait, observe and agree with the others. Narrow side roads in built-up areas can still have priority.
Crossing a priority road with your view blocked by parked vehicles: drive onto the crossroads slowly and carefully.
You must wait when turning out of a farm track, a driveway, a traffic-calmed area, or over a sunken kerbstone.
3-way or 4-way STOP: every vehicle stops. The one that arrived first moves off first, provided it is safe.

Traffic lights: green long time, watch closely and be ready to stop. Amber at 40 km/h with 40 m to go: stop. Amber when you are 10 m away: proceed. Red while turning right: stop. Flashing amber: approach with greater caution and give way if necessary.
Green arrow: you may turn right if no one is obstructed or endangered, especially pedestrians and cross traffic. Stop at the stop line, or before the crossing if there is none.
Lane signals above the road show which lanes are open. You may not use a lane that the signal closes (see the picture pages below).
A police officer's signals beat lights and signs. Police instructions must be obeyed.

Never drive into a crossroads, junction, level crossing or pedestrian crossing if you would have to wait on it in congestion, even on green or with priority. Do not obstruct vehicles with blue lights and siren.
Use the picture pages below for the right-of-way scenes. Each scene shows the correct answer printed under the question.
7: Warning signs (red triangle): children, old people, pedestrian crossing, traffic signals, roundabout, steep slope, bends, merging traffic, wind, sand, animals, level crossings. Reduce speed and be ready to brake.
The red-edged "!" triangle: danger 150 m to 250 m ahead outside built-up areas. Level crossing beacons: three stripes about 240 m, two about 160 m, one about 80 m.

Priority road (diamond sign) gives right of way until it ends. Check bend signs on the priority road: you indicate when you follow it. A narrowing: you may only take precedence when the road is clear, and be ready to stop.
STOP: stop at the stop line, then again where you can see along the road (sight line), and give way. If there is no line, stop again at the sight line.
Mass signs: one sign is about the actual mass, the other about the permissible total mass. Axle weight, width, length and height limits are shown on separate signs.
Speed zone 30 km/h and traffic-calmed areas: watch for pedestrians. End signs cancel the ban. 60 km/h minimum speed signs: you must drive at least that fast, or not use the road.
Parking signs: disabled bays need the permit with the right number, resident bays need a licence with the matching number, signs may allow only light vehicles up to 2.8 t.

Level crossing: wait in front of the level crossing sign when a red light flashes, the barrier is lowering or closed, or a railway worker waves a white-red-white flag or a red lamp. With open barriers approach slowly and look along the line.

Do not enter a crossing if you would have to stop on the rails in a jam. Outside built-up areas, a car with trailer waits immediately after the single-stripe beacon. In a long wait, switch off the engine to save fuel and cut pollution, and put on parking lights in the dark.
A flashing red arrow pointing right: only road users turning right must wait. Cross after a train once the red flashing light goes out.
Use the picture pages below for every sign in the book with its official meaning.
8: Children: reduce speed and be ready to brake. They rush onto the road, turn back for a ball, and look one way and set off. If a ball rolls out, slow down at once.
School and bus stop areas: children run out and across in front of buses. A school bus stopping ahead is dangerous even 80 m away.
Elderly pedestrians: eyesight and hearing are poorer, they react slowly, may stop abruptly or turn back. A pedestrian with a white stick: reduce speed and stop if needed.

Passing a bus at a stop: only at walking speed and only if passengers are not endangered or obstructed. With hazard lights on, drive past at walking speed and stop if necessary. Expect people to cross in front of or behind the bus.

Zebra crossing: approach at moderate speed and wait if needed. No overtaking before or on it, no stopping on it. Take extra care if your view is blocked or another vehicle is waiting. Do not stop on the crossing in congestion.
A cyclist crossing wrongly: let them cross. Mud on the crossing: brake early and stop if needed.
Dogs on a lead can pull a child onto the road. Cyclists are dangerous when they switch to the road without looking. Motorcyclists are overlooked and their speed underestimated.
A truck turning right can swing out to the left first.
9: Pulling out from parked vehicles: your view is limited and approaching drivers see you late. Pulling out of a driveway: you wait, and check for children and pedestrians on the pavement first.
Changing lanes: signal in time and check the traffic behind. Check mirrors and remember the blind angle. Lane ends or blocked: the zipper method, drivers in the continuing lane let others in turn.
Overtaking cyclists and pedestrians: keep at least 1.5 m side distance. 50 cm is not enough. Do not overtake if oncoming traffic makes that impossible.
Never overtake: when you cannot go considerably faster, when the view or traffic situation is unclear, at pedestrian crossings, at blind spots, or just before a crossroads behind a truck.
Finish overtaking before an unbroken line or no-overtaking sign. At 100 km/h behind a 70 km/h truck you need about 800 m before the brow of a hill.

Pull out only if traffic behind and oncoming are not endangered. To end: indicate clearly and in good time, return to the lane without inconveniencing the vehicle you passed. Signal both before pulling out and before pulling in.

Being overtaken: keep as far left as possible, do not speed up. If an overtaking car misjudges, brake and move left. A slow vehicle with a queue must let faster vehicles pass, by using the hard shoulder or a lay-by.

Turning right: check behind, indicate, get in lane, check again just before turning. Give way to oncoming cyclists and vehicles, and to pedestrians crossing the road you enter. Two vehicles turning right generally turn in front of each other.
Turning left into a priority road: watch for vehicles from both sides, and for pedestrians and cyclists on your left or behind you.
The person changing direction must signal. U-turns are forbidden on Highways and clearways. Reversing: look mainly to the rear, also front and sides, and go slowly.
Wrong lane at the lights: carry on and accept the detour. Do not swerve across.
10: No stopping: on level crossings, narrow roads and blind spots, on acceleration/deceleration lanes, between lane dividers with direction arrows, on pedestrian crossings and within 5 m before them, near sharp bends, on freeway/clearway outside parking areas.

No parking: within 5 m before or behind crossroads and junctions, before sunken kerbstones, at taxi ranks, opposite driveways on narrow roads, on priority roads outside built-up areas, within 15 m of a bus stop sign.

Before a railway crossing: 50 m clear outside built-up areas, 5 m inside. If your vehicle hides traffic lights keep 10 m clear. Do not stop within 10 m of a hidden Railway Cross or Stop/Give Way sign.

You are "parked" if you leave the vehicle or stop for more than 3 minutes. At a bus stop you may stop up to 3 minutes if you do not obstruct buses. Taxis may stop in second row to let passengers on or off.

Parking on the left: leave at least 3 m between your vehicle and the lane marking. Parallel parking lanes: in two-way streets only the left one, in one-way streets either. Parking on the right is allowed in one-way streets.

Trailers: a trailer alone may stay on public roads no more than 2 weeks. Trailers over 2 t may be parked in industrial areas on Sundays, public holidays and 22:00 to 06:00. Vehicles up to 3.5 t may use designated footpaths.

Parking disc: you arrive 10:40 in a 2 hour area, set 11:00 (the next half hour mark). Use the parking ticket and do not exceed the time. A broken meter: you may stop only to board, alight, load or unload.
Getting out: check behind and for cyclists before opening the door. Let children out on the pavement side. Passengers watch for traffic on the left side.
Securing: take the key, lock the steering, close windows, lock doors and boot. On a downhill slope: parking brake plus first or reverse (manual), or P and parking brake (automatic).
Breakdown or tyre failure on a Highway: hazard lights, stop as far left as possible, warning triangle about 100 m back. At night also hazard lights and triangle.

Towing: hazard lights on both vehicles, tow-rope or bar clearly marked, max 5 m between the vehicles, tow-rope kept taut. Power steering and servo brakes need much more effort when the engine is off. You need at least class B to tow.
11: Moving from a lit road into an unlit one: your eyes adapt slowly, obstacles and pedestrians are harder to see.
Dazzled by oncoming lights: look to the left-hand edge of the road and slow down, even stop if needed. Do not look at the lights.

Wildlife: dusk and dawn are peak times. Deer come in groups, and stragglers follow. If you cannot avoid a collision: brake, hold the wheel firmly and keep your direction. After a collision stop, hazard lights, make the scene safe, inform police or council.
Full beam: dip for oncoming traffic, when following another vehicle closely, on well-lit roads or at a level crossing. Dipped lights must not dazzle: check height, bulbs and overload.

Fog lights: fog, rain and falling hail when visibility is very low. Rear fog lamps when visibility is under 50 m. Dipped headlights in the daytime when fog, rain or hail cut visibility, in twilight and in dark underpasses. Parking lights alone are not enough when driving in the dark.
Oncoming drivers flash at you: your headlights may be dazzling them or the light range is set wrong. A blue dash light means full beam.
Police: "STOP POLICE" or "Please Follow" lights mean you. A red disc from a car you cannot recognise means follow and stop behind it.
Siren or blue light: clear the way, mount the pavement carefully if necessary. Blue light with no siren: vehicle on duty, give way. Amber flashing: roadworks, accident scene, wide or slow load.
Traffic jam: switch on hazard lights and leave a channel for emergency vehicles.

Accident duties: pull over, inform the police, give your name, address, licence and registration on request. Damaged a parked car and no owner came: leave name and address on it and report to police within 24 hours.

First on the scene of an accident with injured people: make the scene safe, give first aid, call the rescue service and the police. Stop and find out the results, make the scene safe, help the injured.
12: The Central Card-Index for Traffic Offences records criminal traffic offences and offences with an administrative fine. Entries are struck off after two years.
Teaching for hire or reward needs a Driving Instructor Certificate. An expired PSV permit after 25 months means a full test and new medical certificate and fingerprints.
Young drivers crash more because of exuberance, showing off, speed and risk taking, too little experience and over-trust in the car. A driver should ask passengers not to distract them.

Your licence can be reviewed after frequent violations or a permanent handicap. The learner (trial) period is 6 months. Driving without a licence before the test can lead to refusal of the licence because of doubts about character.
13: The owner and the driver are responsible for the roadworthiness of a licensed vehicle. If it stops being roadworthy, take it off the road and continue only after repair. No roadworthiness or no insurance means no public road.
Defects that endanger traffic: worn tyres, defective rear lights, insufficient braking. Check brakes on an unfamiliar vehicle, after long standing and after washing underneath.

Tyres: check pressure regularly including the spare, and adjust for load. Low pressure causes overheating, poor stability, higher fuel use and faster wear. Minimum profile 1.6 mm. Re-conditioned tyres: do not exceed their speed limit and check pressure more often. Emergency wheel: max 80 km/h.

Wet drum brakes: apply the brakes gently while driving slowly. Disc brakes act later on wet roads. Brakes grabbing on one side swing the car out and lengthen braking distance. ASR reduces wheelspin, ABS keeps steering control when braking.
Tyre burst at high speed: throttle down, steer against it, brake cautiously, stop on the hard shoulder with hazard lights and triangle.

Trailer check: lights, brakes (overrun brakes), breakaway cable, jack wheel raised, mirrors, coupling locked. A 600 kg single-axle trailer needs at least 24 kg (4%) on the coupling. Permissible towed load is in the registration certificate, book or manual.

Loads: stowed securely and covered if blowing, never beyond the permissible mass or axle weights, never obstructing the driver. Max width 2.50 m, max height 4.3 m, truck-and-trailer length 20 m. No load beyond the front.

Load beyond the rear: up to 1 m beyond the rear reflectors needs no marker. By day mark with a bright red flag or sign at least 30 x 30 cm. At night a red light or reflector. A red marker light may be at most 1.50 m high. A load more than 40 cm past the side lights needs a white light front and a red light rear.
An overload of only 20% can overstrain brakes, worsen steering and strain parts. Roof loads follow the manual and raise side-wind sensitivity and body roll.

Seat belts on all seats, inside and outside built-up areas, even with air bags. Not needed at walking speed or when parking. Serious or fatal injuries are likely from 30 km/h without a belt. Children travel in an approved child seat or raised seat that fits their height and weight. Truck floor: max 8 persons for work transport.
Class B: light vehicles up to 3,500 kg, towing a trailer up to 750 kg. Check the permissible towed load of your car before you tow, and heavier trailers need class EB.
14: Switch off the engine when waiting long (jam, level crossing). Avoid unnecessary trips and idling. Avoid short trips, full-throttle starts and revving.
Fix a defective exhaust at once: noise and parts falling off. A souped-up engine adds noise and pollutant emission. Dark exhaust smoke means worn or badly tuned engine, have it checked immediately.

Save fuel: drive in the highest sensible gear at low revs, anticipate to avoid braking and accelerating, check tyre pressure, remove the roof rack and unnecessary load, avoid peak hours, use car pools, public transport and park-and-ride.
One drop of oil can pollute up to 600 litres of drinking water. When refuelling do not breathe the fumes and do not top up after the nozzle switches off.
Catalytic converters are damaged by leaded fuel, frequent misfiring, many failed starts and being towed to start.

Towing a trailer: more room needed on turns, less acceleration, hasty steering invites skids, overtaking distance increases. A trailer without brakes lengthens braking: slow down early and use a low gear downhill. Use engine braking by changing down in good time, and engage the clutch gently.

Do not press the clutch and switch off the engine downhill: steering and brake boosters stop working. Degressive braking (hard first, then easing off) shortens braking distance when something blocks the road.

Vehicles with trailers over 7 m combination length on single-lane roads need a longer gap so an overtaker can pull in. Canvas-covered or unloaded high trailers react to side wind. Reversing with poor view: keep sight contact with your guide.

Orange warning plates mean dangerous goods. A white plate with a red L means a beginner is driving. Before driving someone else's car adjust seat, head rest, belt and mirrors. Clean all windows and mirrors before you go. If you dirty the road leaving a field or building site, you must clean it. Secure and report anything that falls off your vehicle.

qs.q: You are approaching a narrow left-hand bend at high speed. Why must you reduce speed already before entering the bend?
opts: Because otherwise you will be thrown 360 Grad straight
Because otherwise you will be thrown out of the bend to the rear
Because otherwise you will be thrown out of the bend to the right

qs.q: Who is responsible for the roadworthiness of a licensed vehicle?
What are the consequences for a person driving a motor vehicle under the influence of drugs (e.g. Hashish, Heroin, Cocaine)?
Moisture impaired the action of drum brakes on your vehicle. What should you do?
opts: Drive with high speed and apply the brakes frequently
Cautiously apply the brakes whilst driving slowly

qs.q: Above which alcohol level in your blood can you expect your fitness to drive to be impaired considerably?
How long can hashish and its catabolic (decomposition products) be detected in the urine?
What effects can drugs have whilst driving?
opts: Drugs are essential to pass the driving test

qs.q: One of your tyre burst whilst travelling at high speed on a highway. What do you do?
opts: Brake harsh and steer immediately to the right to keep direction of travel
Brake carefully, switch on your hazard warning lights, hold the steering wheel firmly, keep direction of travel towards the hard shoulder smoothly and place the warning triangle

qs.q: What must you remember particularly when driving with re-conditioned tyres?
opts: Re-conditioned tyres are not permitted by law
Re-conditioned tyres have the same life span than new tyres
The maximum permissible speed for these tyres may not be exceeded

qs.q: When you are not allowed to use a motor vehicle on public roads?
opts: When the vehicle is older than 10 years

qs.q: Participating in road traffic requires caution at all times and consideration towards other road users. What does this mean for you?
opts: You should never drive at night
You may trust other road users
You must drive always with foresight

qs.q: What can cause a dangerous situation?
opts: Driving during the day without headlights

qs.q: What can cause a dangerous situation?
opts: Brakes which engage on all four wheels

qs.q: You had to obtain an expert opinion because of a technical modification to your vehicle. What are you required to do?
opts: Obtaining a roadworthiness report is enough
The certificate on the opinion including new roadworthiness report must be carried and the vehicle document must be corrected

qs.q: The suspension of your motor vehicle has been lowered and an expert opinion must be obtained. When is this required?
opts: Before intending to alter the vehicle

qs.q: What is required when your vehicle is no longer covered by a motor vehicle insurance?
opts: The insurance company has to provide a new and insured vehicle
The vehicle must be given back to the insurance company
The vehicle must be de-registered at the licensing registration office

qs.q: What leads frequently to serious accidents when overtaking on highways?
opts: Driving with enough distance to the vehicle in front
Keeping a close eye on the traffic situation behind
Driving too close to the vehicle in front

qs.q: You want to leave the Highway. What must you do?
opts: Reduce speed in the vertex of the exit lane
Use the left-hand lane early enough and indicate in good time
Increase the speed before reaching the exit lane

qs.q: What must be remembered here?
opts: The far left space is only for agricultural vehicles
It is forbidden to stop on the right of the white roadway boundary marking
Slow moving vehicles are not permitted to use this road

qs.q: Where is fast driving particularly dangerous?
opts: On narrow roads and at blind spots
After having passed a level crossings

qs.q: Which dangers can arise in this residential area?
opts: Well traffic trained children on the road

qs.q: Who has stopped incorrectly?
opts: The (yellow) vehicle behind the pedestrian crossing
The (red) vehicle in front of the pedestrian crossing

qs.q: What must you do in this situation being dazzled by oncoming traffic?
opts: Look to the right-hand edge of the roadway and if necessary, increase your speed
Look to the left-hand edge of the roadway and if necessary, reduce your speed
Use your horn and switch-on your headlights too

qs.q: A traffic jam is building up here. What must you do?
opts: Stop immediately if you hear an emergency vehicle
Drive as close as possible to the vehicle in front
Switch on your hazard warning lights to warn vehicles following you

qs.q: You are the first person to arrive at the scene of an accident with injured persons. In which order to you proceed?
opts: Call the rescue service only and leave the accident scene
Make the scene of the accident safe, give first aid, call the rescue service and the police
Ask other road users to take the necessary action

qs.q: Which conduct is correct?
opts: The oncoming cyclist may proceed first
I am allowed to cross the crossroads first
The truck must wait till the crossing is free

qs.q: Which conduct is correct?
opts: The oncoming motorcyclist must wait for me because he intends to turn left
The oncoming motorcyclist may proceed first

qs.q: What happens as a result of tyre pressure being well below the recommended levels?
What must you remember when re-fuelling?
opts: I always should drive with half filled tank
I always should re-fuel up to the top level
Do not breath in any fuel fumes

qs.q: The engine and exhaust system of your vehicle have been *souped-up*. What could be the reason?
opts: Driving always with high speed on long distances
qs.note: Your stencil marks this answer, but none of the options match the manual, which says a souped-up engine and exhaust give more noise and more pollutant emission. Learn the marked answer for the test and ask your instructor about it.

qs.q: Alterations to your vehicle have resulted to impound the car by the Police. What are the consequences?
opts: Demand for a new and higher insurance coverage
Issuing fines for such traffic offence plus a new driving test
Issuing fines for such traffic offence plus demerit points

qs.q: You are driving on a road outside a built-up area with three lanes in each direction. Individual vehicles are travelling well spaced out in the far left-hand lane. Which lane may you use continuosly?
opts: I have to follow the vehicles travelling in the far left-hand lane

qs.q: You want to leave the Highway. What must you do?
opts: Reduce speed in the vertex of the exit lane
Use the left-hand lane early enough and indicate in good time
Increase the speed before reaching the exit lane

qs.q: What must you remember when leaving the Highway?
opts: That vehicles in front will overtake
That the bend will become wide enough to speed up again
That a traffic jam is likely on the bend

qs.q: What does this traffic sign mean?
opts: The shoulder should be used in case of oncoming traffic
The shoulder should be used for parking
The shoulder beside the roadway is not strong (hard) enough

qs.q: What must you expect when you see this traffic sign?
opts: Vehicles in front may speed-up suddenly
That there are 3 vehicles in front

qs.q: What does this traffic sign indicate?
opts: Coordinated traffic lights if driving at the average speed of 55 km/h

qs.q: Your vehicle has an engine failure on the Highway. What must you remember when having it towed away?
opts: During towing, both vehicles must use their hazard warning lights
I do need driving licence class EC for towing occasionally a light vehicle
Only certified companies are allowed to tow away break- downs from a Highway

qs.q: What dangers could arise if you drive over this damaged part of the road?
opts: Axles of the vehicles are not affected
Your vehicle could go into a skid
The potholes will become smaller with increased traffic

qs.q: Which dangers can arise in this residential area?
opts: Well traffic trained children on the road

qs.q: You are travelling at high speed. Where in particular can obstructions suddenly appear?
opts: By waiting vehicles in side roads
By vehicles following with the same speed

qs.q: For which motor vehicles is the recommended speed on Highways intended?
